senses.def: (title for God; a Greek transliteration of an Aramaic word meaning ‘father’) one who combines aspects of supernatural authority and care for his people
senses.comment: Though there is a widespread tendency to preserve the Aramaic transliteration in the form of either abba or aba, there are frequent dangers in doing so, since the transliterated form may actually correspond to another word in a receptor language and thus provide an obstacle to proper understanding. In general, there is no point in a translation of ἀββά, since the resulting expression would simply be Father Father. Accordingly, in many languages the combination of Abba, Father is simply reduced to Father. In a number of languages, however, a vocative form (that is to say, a form used in direct address) is different from a form used in speaking about God as Father. It is, of course, essential to employ the appropriate grammatical form.|In a number of languages it is necessary to distinguish clearly between ‘Father’ when referring to the heavenly Father and ‘father’ as a reference to a human father. The use of capitalization is quite satisfactory for the individual who is reading a text but not for one who is hearing it read, and since more people hear a text read than read it for themselves, it is essential that the reference of ‘Father’ be clear. In order to identify the use of ‘Father’ as a title for God, it is possible in many languages to use ‘Father in heaven’ or ‘Father above’ or ‘Father God.’|In some languages it may even be necessary to identify the ‘Father’ as the creator and therefore employ a phrase such as ‘our Father who created us.’|A particularly complicating factor involved in the use of ‘Father’ as a title for God is its occurrence without a pronominal reference as to whose father is involved. For example, in a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘father’ without indicating whose father, because a person does not become a father except by some relationship to another individual. Therefore, one must always speak of ‘my father’ or ‘his father’ and never simply ‘the father.’ In passages in which Jesus is speaking of ‘the Father’ in relationship to himself, it is necessary usually to employ a phrase such as ‘my Father.’ When, however, ‘Father’ is used as a title for ‘God’ in his relationship to people generally, then one may speak of ‘our Father’ (normally with an inclusive first person plural pronoun if the language in question makes a distinction between inclusive and exclusive first person plural pronoun referents).

senses.subdomain: Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀγρυπνέω ‘to keep oneself awake,’ not occurring in the NT) to make an effort to learn of what might be a potential future threat
glosses: to be on the lookout for

senses.def: to take care of or to look after, with the implication of continuous and wakeful concern for
a person who was healed by Peter
a relatively large building normally used for legal hearings, though possibly also employed for more general purposes
senses.comment: In a number of languages ἀκροατήριον may be rendered as ‘a large hall’ or ‘a place where many people could gather together’ or ‘a building where many people could sit to listen.’

senses.def: pertaining to not losing the wonderful, pristine character of something
to make known that which has presumably been hidden or unknown previously
to cause people to rebel against or to reject authority
a Jewish high priest
(derivative of ἀποδείκνυμι[a] to demonstrate, to show, 28.50) the means by which one knows that something is a fact.
the role of one who has been commissioned and sent as a special messenger
senses.comment: See also ἀπόστολος[a] (53.74).

senses.def: to be sufficient or adequate for a particular purpose, with the implication of leading to satisfaction
to be happy or content as the result of having what one desires or needs to be
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘to be content’ is expressed negatively, for example, ‘to not complain.’ In other instances, one may be forced to employ a type of direct or indirect discourse, for example, ‘to acknowledge that it is enough’ or ‘to say, It is all that is needed.’

senses.def: a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite
the state of being content with one’s circumstances or lot in life
a state of adequacy or sufficiency
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of this expression in 2 Corinthians 9:8 may be ‘always having all that you need’ or, stated negatively, ‘not lacking in anything.’

senses.def: branch of the palm tree (φοῖνιξ)
senses.comment: βάϊον is a technical term meaning ‘palm branch,’ and in John 12:13 τῶν φοινίκων ‘of palm trees’ may have been added redundantly, since the term βάϊον may not have been regarded as sufficiently well known to readers.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: (derivative of βραδύς ‘slow,’ 67.123) extending of a period of time, with the implication of slowness and/or delay
(derivative of γεννάω[b] ‘to give birth,’ 23.52) that which has been produced or born of a living creature
senses.comment: In some languages it may be possible to translate this phrase in Matthew 3:7 more or less literally, for example, ‘the offspring of vipers,’ in which ‘vipers’ means poisonous snakes, but in other languages this would be impossible, and one must therefore use ‘little snakes.’ For another interpretation of γέννημα in Matthew 3:7, see 58.26.

senses.def: a kind or class of persons, with the implication of possessing certain derived characteristics
glosses: one who has the characteristics of
senses.comment: For another interpretation of γέννημα in Matthew 3:7, see 23.53.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of δάκνω ‘to bite,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause personal harm to someone

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to the second of two days
senses.comment: Some persons have interpreted δευτεραῖος as a period of two days, so that one may translate ‘after two days we came to Puteoli.’ Though general Greek usage does not seem to substantiate this meaning for δευτεραῖος, the context of Acts 28:13 may involve a span of two days.

senses.def: the content of thinking and reasoning
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to find noun-like words for thinking or reasoning and therefore it may be necessary to use a verb equivalent throughout. For example, in Luke 11:17 one may translate as ‘but Jesus knew what they were thinking.’

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: a period of two successive years
a Christian woman in Joppa who was known for charitable works; her Aramaic name was Ταβιθά (93.355)
(derivative of ἐγκάθημαι ‘to lie in a crouched position,’ not occurring in the NT) one whose task it is to obtain information surreptitiously
to come to or to arrive at the scene of action
welcome extended to a person on the occasion of a visit, with probable focus upon the ready acceptance
to depart from a place without being noticed
senses.comment: In rendering ἐκνεύω in John 5:13 one may say ‘Jesus left and no one saw him’ or ‘no one saw Jesus departing.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἐλεάω ‘to show mercy,’ 88.76) pertaining to showing mercy
to breathe upon something
senses.comment: The process of breathing on someone may have very important symbolic implications. In some instances this can be related to a blessing, as in John 20:22, but in some languages the act of breathing on a person almost inevitably suggests some harmful influence, often connected with the use of black magic. It may therefore be important to select some less specific term so as to avoid a symbolic meaning which would considerably distort the significance of this one passage in which ἐμφυσάω occurs in the NT.

senses.def: extension from a source, with the point of reference near the speaker
a reference to reason or source

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to ill-treat someone with contempt
glosses: to ill-treat and look down upon
senses.comment: Because of the complex nature of the meaning of ἐξουδενέω, it is often possible to translate the term with a semantic doublet, for example, ‘to look down upon and to ill-treat.’ This double meaning can be readily derived from the literal rendering ‘to regard as nothing.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to mistreat, with the implication of threats and abuse
pertaining to yearning affection for someone
cardinal number, where there are seven thousand instances of a countable entity

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: to be pleased with something or someone, with the implication of resulting pleasure

senses.subdomain: Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
senses.def: to take pleasure in something in that it fulfills one’s desires
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to enjoy’ is ‘to make someone happy’ or ‘to make one feel good.’ This expression in 2 Thessalonians 2:12 may be rendered as ‘but when they are sinning, they feel good’ or ‘but to sin makes them happy.’

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to think of something as being good, better, or preferable
to express gratitude for benefits or blessings
senses.comment: Thanks is often expressed in highly idiomatic ways. For example, in some languages one says thank you by saying ‘may God pay you.’ Such a phrase may be so standardized as to even be used in expressing thankfulness to God himself. In other instances, thankfulness may be expressed as ‘you have made my heart warm.’

senses.def: to be thankful on the basis of some received benefit

senses.subdomain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View
senses.def: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something
to so influence others as to cause them to follow a recommended course of action
senses.comment: In some languages it is difficult to distinguish readily between expressions for ‘leading’ and those which refer to ‘ruling’ or ‘governing,’ but it is important to try to distinguish clearly between these two different sets of interpersonal relations. In some languages, the concept of ‘leading’ can be expressed by ‘showing how to’ or ‘demonstrating how one ought to.’ In other languages it is possible to speak of ‘leading’ as simply ‘going ahead of,’ but too often such an expression may designate only ‘a scout’ who goes ahead to see whether things are safe, or it may refer only to a person who insists on his prerogative as the most distinguished person in a group.

senses.def: to rule over, with the implication of providing direction and leadership
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to express the concept of ‘ruling’ by some form of ‘command,’ for example, ‘he commands people what they must do’ or ‘he orders people’ or ‘he is the chief over people.’

senses.def: a chemical found in pale yellow mineral form; burns readily in air and is found in regions of vulcanic activity such as the Dead Sea area; causes land to be infertile; associated with punishment from God
senses.comment: In the NT θεῖον is always associated in some way with fire and refers to the kinds of burning hot rocks involved in volcanic eruptions. The closest equivalent in a number of languages is ‘burning stones’ or ‘fiery hot stones’ or ‘fiery red stones.’

senses.def: sudden and violent gusts of winds, often from varied directions
senses.comment: In a number of languages a strong wind which causes the waves or a storm on water must be referred to by a special term. Compare, for example, the English term squall; this would mean a wind of relatively short duration but sufficiently intense so as to create relatively high waves.

senses.def: the means by which sins are forgiven
senses.comment: Though some traditional translations render ἱλαστήριον as ‘propitiation,’ this involves a wrong interpretation of the term in question. Propitiation is essentially a process by which one does a favor to a person in order to make him or her favorably disposed, but in the NT God is never the object of propitiation since he is already on the side of people. ἱλασμός and ἱλαστήριον[a] denote the means of forgiveness and not propitiation.

senses.def: an OT prophet (Matthew 12:39)
an alternative form for Ἰωάννης[e] (John 1:42, apparatus)
to cause harm or injury to someone or something (a highly generic meaning involving a wide range of harm and injury)
senses.comment: In translating terms meaning ‘to harm’ or ‘to injure,’ it may be necessary to specify suffering, for example, ‘to cause people to suffer’ or ‘to cause people to have pain.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to cause a person’s attitude to be bad against) to cause someone to have hostile feelings of dislike toward someone
to destroy something by burning
senses.comment: See comments on terms for burning in 14.63 and 14.65.

senses.def: to watch or observe secretly and with presumed evil intent
senses.comment: The phrase ‘to spy out our freedom’ may be rendered as ‘to observe how free we are as spies would do.’

senses.def: to express an unusually high degree of confidence in someone or something being exceptionally noteworthy
senses.comment: Whether in any particular context the boasting is legitimate or not depends upon what is boasted about. In a number of languages, however, quite different terms are employed, depending upon the differing degrees of justification for such boasting.

senses.def: (derivative of καυχάομαι ‘to boast,’ 33.368) the referent of boasting, namely, that which one boasts about
the state of being rightfully proud
an instrument used for locking and unlocking doors and gates
senses.comment: In rendering Revelation 9:1 it may not be possible to speak of ‘the key to the abyss,’ but rather ‘the key to the entrance to the abyss’ or ‘the key used in opening or closing the gate to the abyss.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of κλείς[a] ‘key,’ 6.220) a means of acquiring something
senses.comment: One may also translate this expression in Luke 11:52 as ‘you have kept to yourselves the key to knowledge’ or ‘… the means by which one may gain understanding.’

senses.def: a violent and extensive slaughter, especially associated with armed conflicts
(derivative of κτάομαι ‘to acquire,’ 57.58) that which is owned or possessed (usually land)

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.comment: The context of Romans 3:13 is highly figurative, and in a number of languages it may be necessary either to change the metaphor into a simile, for example, ‘their throat is like an open tomb,’ or to employ a somewhat altered equivalent, for example, ‘their speech is full of deadly deceit.’

senses.def: a long weapon with sharpened end used for piercing by thrusting or as a projectile by hurling
senses.comment: Perhaps in John 19:34 ‘spear point’

senses.def: (derivative of μακροθυμία ‘patience,’ 25.167) pertaining to being patient
senses.comment: In Acts 26:3 it may be necessary in some languages to spell out the implications of μακροθύμως, for example, ‘therefore I beg you to listen to me without interrupting’ or ‘… without stopping me.’

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to think about something in such a way as to make an appropriate response
senses.comment: It may be possible to render ‘is God concerned about oxen’ (1 Corinthians 9:9) as ‘is God thinking about doing something about oxen.’

senses.def: to be particularly concerned about something, with the implication of some apprehension
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to be concerned about’ may be simply ‘to think about,’ and the negative might be merely ‘not to let something enter one’s head.’

senses.def: a relationship involving shared purposes and activity
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 6:14 δικαιοσύνη and ἀνομία refer to ‘those who do right’ and ‘those who do wrong.’ In fact, in a number of languages one can only translate this expression in 2 Corinthians 6:14 as ‘how can a person who does right and one who does wrong join in a partnership?’ or ‘how can one who does right and one who does wrong work together?’ In this same verse κοινωνία (see 34.5) has a meaning closely corresponding to μετοχή, and similarly φῶς and σκότος refer respectively to ‘those who live in the light’ and ‘those who live in darkness,’ paralleling closely the distinction between δικαιοσύνη and ἀνομία.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of μοιχεύω ‘to commit adultery,’ 88.276) a woman who commits adultery
(a figurative extension of meaning of the substantive μοιχαλίς ‘adulteress,’ 88.278) pertaining to being unfaithful to one’s earlier and true beliefs
one who works on a ship
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ναύτης is ‘one who handles the ropes’ or ‘one who works on a boat.’

senses.def: to misappropriate funds for one’s own benefit
to manage and provide for a household
glosses: to be in charge of a household
senses.comment: In biblical times a household would consist of more than the nuclear family, that is to say, more than simply husband, wife, and children, for servants, slaves, and permanent hired workers living with the family would be regarded as a part of the total household.

senses.def: a slave of Philemon

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.comment: In some languages a distinction is made between bones as a part of a living body and bones from which the meat has been removed, for example, the bones of a skeleton. Note, for example, the reference to τὰ ὀστέα as the bones of Joseph in Hebrews 11:22.

senses.def: (diminutive of παῖς[a] ‘child,’ 9.41, but in the NT παιδίον has seemingly lost at least most of this diminutive force, but may have retained some implications of affectionate concern or interest) a child, normally below the age of puberty
(diminutive of παῖς[b] ‘child,’ 10.36, but with the loss of at least most of the diminutive meaning) one’s immediate offspring
senses.comment: One need not assume in Luke 11:7 that the children were in the same bed with their father. One may render this passage simply as ‘I have gone to bed and so have my children’ or ‘I am already in bed and so are my children,’ but see 6.108.

senses.subdomain: Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
senses.def: (extension of meaning of παιδίον[a] ‘child,’ 9.42) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
senses.comment: In a number of languages παιδία in John 21:5 is better rendered as ‘my good friends’ or ‘my dear friends’ or ‘my dear comrades.’ In this context, not age, but the connotation of affection and endearment is in focus.

senses.def: (a technical, nautical term) to sail along beside some object

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a person who habitually drinks too much and thus becomes a drunkard
to believe in something or someone to the extent of placing reliance or trust in or on
senses.comment: In a number of languages trust or reliance is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to lean one’s weight on’ or ‘to hang upon’ or ‘to place oneself in the hands of.’

senses.def: a person greeted in Romans 16:12
a quantity of space completely occupied by something
a totality which has been brought to completion
pertaining to a particularly large number of objects or events
to move from one place to another, with the possible implication of continuity and distance
to move a considerable distance, either with a single destination or from one destination to another in a series
to move away from a reference point
to live or behave in a customary manner, with possible focus upon continuity of action
to depart from life, as a euphemistic expression for death
to provide for the needs of others, with the implication of anticipating such a need
senses.comment: It may be possible to translate προβλέπομαι in Hebrews 11:40 as ‘to provide for by foreseeing’ or ‘… by determining in advance’ (see 30.100).

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to choose or select in advance of some other event
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand προβλέπομαι in Hebrews 11:40 as meaning ‘to decide in advance’ (compare the meanings in 30.84) or ‘to provide for’ (35.35).

senses.def: to pay out or spend in addition
to run ahead of someone else, with the implication of arriving at a destination sooner
the young of a donkey ὄνος
senses.comment: As in the case of ὄνος ‘donkey’ (4.31), a number of languages make a distinction either in form or in terms for the young of a donkey based upon distinctions in sex.

senses.def: (a Greek transliteration of a Hebrew word meaning armies and used with κύριος[a] Lord, 12.9, as a title for God) pertaining to one who has overwhelming power
glosses: One who is powerful over all

senses.def: a fine grade of wheat flour

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause to be stubborn and obstinate, especially with regard to the truth
senses.comment: In the expression σκληρύνω τὰς καρδίας ‘to cause the hearts to be obstinate’ in Hebrews 3:8, καρδία must be understood as ‘the inner self’ (see 26.3) and as such the addition of καρδία merely reinforces the meaning of the verb σκληρύνω.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to be stubborn, in the sense of refusing to believe
a jar regularly used for wine, but in the NT it refers to the jar in which manna was kept permanently

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: a female member of an extended family or clan
to be encouraged at the same time with someone else
glosses: to be encouraged at the same time

senses.def: to accompany someone, with explicit marking of association
a city in Samaria

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a very short extent of time
senses.comment: In 2 Peter 2:1 ταχινός may refer to the swift nature of the destruction or to the fact that destruction comes after a relatively brief period of time.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time
to punish, with the implication of causing people to suffer what they deserve

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to live a life of luxury, usually associated with intemperate feasting and drinking
glosses: to live a life of luxury

senses.def: an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in 78.31 primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
to cause great annoyance to and thus to wear someone out
glosses: to wear someone down by annoying

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὑπωπιάζω ‘to strike the eye,’ not occurring in the NT) to keep one’s body under complete control, with the implication of rough treatment given to the body, possibly as an aspect of discipline (a meaning evidently taken from the language of prize-fighting)
affection for people in general

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to show friendly concern for someone
pertaining to understanding resulting from insight and wisdom

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: the coldest season of the year
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be important to translate χειμών[a] as simply ‘the time of the cold rains.’ Such rains may actually occur during the growing season or as a part of the rainy season. In semi-tropical areas, however, the cold rains do normally occur in what is regarded as the winter, while the warm rains occur in the summer. See also discussion at 67.163.

senses.def: stormy weather involving strong wind, overcast sky, and often cold temperature; thunder and lightning may also be present
senses.comment: The principal difficulty involved in translating χειμών[b] is the fact that in so many languages there are quite distinct terms for various kinds of bad weather or storms. Furthermore, the location of such bad weather will also influence significantly the terms which may be used. For example, stormy weather over the open sea may require quite a different term from what would be used in speaking of a similar kind of storm over the land. In addition, storms which are accompanied by rain may also be referred to by different terms from those which involve wind without rain. Accordingly, one must carefully examine each biblical context in which χειμών[b] is employed and determine what would be the most satisfactory expression in the receptor language. For example, in Matthew 16:3 the reference is to a windstorm accompanied by clouds and moving over land, while in Acts 27:20 the reference is to a storm of long duration which takes place over a body of water.

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea
senses.def: dry land, in contrast with the sea
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate Matthew 14:24 as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in Acts 27:27 one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

senses.def: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration
glosses: district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
senses.comment: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

senses.subdomain: Areas Which Are Uninhabited or Only Sparsely Populated
senses.def: a rural area in contrast with a population center
senses.comment: A rural area is often identified by a term or phrase meaning ‘extension of fields’ or ‘place of field after field’ or ‘area of farms.’

senses.def: land under cultivation or used for pasture

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the inhabitants of a region
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of ‘a region going out’ (Mark 1:5), since the term for ‘region’ cannot substitute for ‘the people of the region.’ Therefore, all such references must be made personal.
